course_overview.title: Understanding the Cycle of Abuse
course_overview.target_audience: General Public, Mental Health Advocates, Social Work Students, Counseling Trainees, or Support Group Facilitators.
course_overview.content_warning: This lesson discusses interpersonal violence, emotional manipulation, and relationship trauma. Please ensure you practice self-care while engaging with this material. If you or someone you know needs immediate assistance, contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-SAFE or text "START" to 88788).

learning_objectives: Identify and explain the 4 core stages of Lenore Walker’s Cycle of Abuse framework.
Differentiate between subtle behavioral tactics (e.g., gaslighting, isolation) and distinct cycle phases.
Analyze real-world scenarios to trace the progression of abusive dynamics.
Apply safety-planning and supportive intervention strategies to assist individuals navigating abusive relationships.

ai_teacher_facilitator_profile.tone: Empathetic, calm, professional, objective, and supportive.
behavioral_guidelines: Maintain a safe, non-judgmental space for learners exploring heavy emotional material.
Pause for participant reflection during interactive segments and prompt critical thinking without pushing personal disclosures.
Reinforce safety resources whenever acute distress indicators or real-world safety themes arise.

facilitator_dialogue_flow.script: Hello everyone, and welcome. Today we are exploring a sensitive yet vital topic: understanding the cycle of abuse based on Dr. Lenore Walker's foundational 1979 framework. Before we begin, please remember to take care of your emotional well-being. If you or anyone you know requires immediate support, confidential help is available via the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-SAFE or by texting 'START' to 88788. Let's move forward with empathy, respect, and a commitment to learning.

Now that we've mapped out the four stages—Tension Building, the Acute Incident, Reconciliation, and Calm—let's check our understanding. How do these phases interact over time without outside intervention? Take a moment to review Activity 1 in your workspace.

Let's review the scenario analysis regarding Alex and Jordan. Notice how subtle microaggressions in Phase 1 quickly escalate into acute incidents in Phase 2. As an AI facilitator, I encourage you to consider how external support structures can break this repetitive loop safely.

sections.title: Introduction to Lenore Walker’s Cycle of Abuse
sections.content: Developed by psychologist Dr. Lenore Walker in 1979, the Cycle of Abuse model illustrates how domestic violence and emotional abuse often follow a repeating, predictable pattern. Rather than being constant physical or emotional conflict, abusive relationships typically oscillate between periods of intense conflict, brief relief, and rebuilding tension.

sections.title: Deep Dive into the 4 Phases

phases.characteristics: Microaggressions, walking on eggshells, unpredictable mood swings, passive-aggressive remarks, or excessive control.
phases.victim_experience: High anxiety, attempts to appease the partner, hyper-vigilance, feeling that a blowup is inevitable.

phases.characteristics: Outburst of abusive behavior. This can be physical, emotional, sexual, verbal, financial, or digital (e.g., excessive monitoring, extreme humiliation, physical destruction of belongings, threats).
phases.victim_experience: Trauma, fear, dissociation, shock, survival mode.

phases.characteristics: Apologies, gift-giving, declarations of love, promises to change, shifting blame to external stress (e.g., job pressure, alcohol), or mini-breakthroughs ("I'm seeking help").
phases.victim_experience: Relief, hope, cognitive dissonance, guilt, believing the partner's positive traits represent their 'true' self.

phases.characteristics: The relationship appears stable and peaceful. The abusive partner acts normal, and the abuse is minimized, ignored, or reframed.
phases.victim_experience: False sense of security, dropping boundaries or plans to leave, lingering subconscious stress.

sections.key_takeaway: Over time, without intervention, the Calm/Honeymoon phases become shorter or disappear entirely, and the intensity of the Tension and Incident phases increases.

interactive_activities.title: Self-Reflection & Knowledge Check
interactive_activities.task: Read each statement and identify which phase of the Cycle of Abuse it represents.

items.statement: "He brought me flowers, sobbed, and promised he would start therapy if I gave him one last chance."
"I try not to bring up money or play music too loudly when they come home from work because I don't want to set them off."
"Things have been completely fine for two weeks. It feels like the fight last month never even happened."

interactive_activities.title: Real-World Scenario Analysis
interactive_activities.scenario: Alex and Jordan have been dating for two years. Recently, Jordan started demanding to see Alex’s text messages and making sarcastic comments about Alex’s family. Alex notices feeling nervous every afternoon before Jordan gets home from work. Last night, after Alex spent 10 minutes talking to a colleague after work, Jordan threw a glass against the wall, shouted insults, and locked Alex out of the bedroom. This morning, Jordan brought Alex breakfast in bed, apologized profusely while crying, said work stress caused the outburst, and bought Alex a new laptop to 'make up for the drama.'

guided_discussion_questions.question: Question A: What specific indicators highlight the Tension Building phase in this scenario?
guided_discussion_questions.guidance: Digital monitoring (demanding text messages) and physiological hyper-vigilance (feeling nervous every afternoon before arrival).

guided_discussion_questions.question: Question B: What tactic is Jordan using in the morning to keep Alex from re-evaluating the relationship?
guided_discussion_questions.guidance: Love bombing, gift-giving (new laptop), externalizing blame onto job stress, and tearful apologies.

guided_discussion_questions.question: Question C: How might a supportive friend intervene effectively without putting Alex in danger?
guided_discussion_questions.guidance: Listening without judgment, validating feelings, avoiding direct hostility toward the partner that could isolate Alex, and providing safety resources.

formative_quiz.question: What is the primary function of the Reconciliation (Honeymoon) phase for the abusive partner?

options.B: To regain control and re-establish the victim's hope in the relationship.
options.C: To prove that the victim was responsible for the incident.
options.D: To show genuine long-term psychological change.

formative_quiz.explanation: The reconciliation phase builds hope and emotional attachment, making it difficult for the victim to exit the relationship.

formative_quiz.question: Which of the following is true about how the Cycle of Abuse evolves over time?

options.A: The calm phase expands until the cycle disappears on its own.
options.B: The cycle remains completely identical in length and intensity indefinitely.
options.C: The time between incidents often shrinks, and abuse frequently escalates in severity.
options.D: The tension building phase disappears completely after the first incident.

formative_quiz.explanation: Without external intervention or accountability, abusive cycles typically shorten in length and increase in severity.

formative_quiz.question: What does 'walking on eggshells' refer to during the Tension Building phase?

options.A: The physical destruction of property in the home.
options.B: The victim constantly modifying their behavior to avoid provoking an abusive outburst.
options.D: The cooling-off period following an acute incident.

formative_quiz.explanation: 'Walking on eggshells' describes the hyper-vigilance and continuous anxiety felt when trying to prevent an outburst.

case_study.title: Maya's Story
case_study.description: Maya has been married to Sam for three years. Sam controls all household finances and requires Maya to send photos showing her location when she isn't home. Last Friday, Sam accused Maya of flirting with a grocery clerk, yelled at her for an hour, and smashed her smartphone. The next day, Sam cleaned the entire house, took Maya out for a fine dinner, and promised to attend anger management classes. Maya confides in you: 'Sam is just really under a lot of pressure at work. When things are good, Sam is the kindest person I know. I think if I just become better at communicating, this won't happen again.'

assessment_deliverables.instruction: Map at least three specific actions from Maya's story to their corresponding phase in the Cycle of Abuse.

key_mappings.tension_building: Financial control and mandatory location tracking via photos.
key_mappings.incident: Accusations of flirting, an hour of yelling, and smashing the smartphone.
key_mappings.reconciliation: House cleaning, fine dinner, promises of anger management, and shifting blame to work pressure.

assessment_deliverables.instruction: Explain why Maya believes 'if I just become better at communicating, this won't happen again' based on the psychological impacts of the cycle.
assessment_deliverables.analysis_explanation: This reflects cognitive dissonance and internalized self-blame. The reconciliation phase manufactures hope, causing the victim to believe the abusive partner's gentle facade is their true nature and attributing the abuse to temporary external triggers.

assessment_deliverables.instruction: Write a short script (3–5 sentences) showing how you would respond to Maya with empathy, validating her feelings while avoiding blame or pushing dangerous immediate ultimatums.
assessment_deliverables.script_example: Maya, thank you for trusting me enough to share what you are going through. What you described—having your phone smashed and living under constant surveillance—sounds terrifying and deeply exhausting. Please know that you did not cause Sam's outburst, no matter how stressful work might be. I care about your safety and want you to know I am here to support you whenever you are ready to talk.
